item.title: Fugu Preparation Class in Shimonoseki — Guide
item.description: Because fugu can be lethal if prepared wrongly, only chefs with a special licence earned through rigorous training and examination may handle and serve it — and in Shimonoseki, the heart of Japan’s fugu trade, some venues let curious visitors get a hands-on glimpse of that craft. A fugu preparation experience typically involves watching or trying, under close expert supervision, how the fish is cleaned, how its toxic parts are carefully removed and set aside, and how the flesh is sliced into the famous wafer-thin sashimi — before, of course, eating the results.

item.title: Kanmon Strait Fireworks Festival, Shimonoseki — Guide
item.description: The Kanmon Strait Fireworks Festival is one of the largest and most spectacular fireworks displays in western Japan, held each summer over the narrow strait between Shimonoseki and Kitakyushu in Kyushu. What makes it special is that both cities launch simultaneously from opposite shores, sending tens of thousands of shells bursting over the water in a friendly cross-strait rivalry, their light doubled by reflection on the sea and framed by the great Kanmon Bridge.

item.title: Karato Market: Shimonoseki's Fresh Seafood Market — Guide
item.description: Karato Market is Shimonoseki’s lively fish market and one of the best places in Yamaguchi to eat superb seafood cheaply. On weekends and holidays it hosts the celebrated ‘Iki-iki Bakangai’, a sushi and street-food event where dozens of stalls sell fresh nigiri, fugu sashimi, seafood bowls and fried treats by the piece — you take a tray, buy what catches your eye, and eat overlooking the Kanmon Strait. Shimonoseki lands more fugu (blowfish) than anywhere in Japan, so this is the place to try it affordably alongside sea bream, tuna and local catches.

item.title: Shimonoseki and the Kanmon Strait — Guide
item.description: The Kanmon Strait is the narrow, fast-flowing channel that separates Honshu from Kyushu at Japan’s western end, with the port city of Shimonoseki on one side and Kitakyushu on the other, barely a kilometre apart. It has been a strategic waterway for centuries — the site of the decisive 1185 sea battle that ended the Genpei War, and later of the town’s opening to foreign trade. Today the strait is crossed by the soaring Kanmon Bridge, by rail and road tunnels, and remarkably by a pedestrian tunnel you can walk under the sea from one prefecture to another.

item.title: Shimonoseki Fugu Festival — Guide
item.description: As Japan’s fugu capital, Shimonoseki celebrates its signature blowfish with seasonal festivals and events, especially as the fugu season peaks in autumn and winter. These gatherings — held at the port, markets and temples — bring together fugu tastings and cheap eats, market stalls, and even Shinto rituals giving thanks for the harvest and praying for safety, reflecting the fish’s deep importance to the city. For visitors, a fugu festival is a lively, affordable and atmospheric way to enjoy the delicacy alongside locals, sampling fugu dishes at their seasonal best in the very city that made them famous.

item.title: Shimonoseki Fugu: Eating Blowfish in Its Capital — Guide
item.description: Shimonoseki is the fugu capital of Japan, landing the great majority of the nation’s blowfish and treating it as the city’s signature delicacy. Fugu is famous as much for its danger as its taste — parts of the fish are highly poisonous, so only specially licensed chefs may prepare it — but in expert hands it is utterly safe and prized for its clean, delicate flavour and firm texture. The classic way to eat it is ‘fugu sashi’, wafer-thin translucent slices arranged like petals, followed by ‘fugu-chiri’ hotpot, deep-fried karaage, and grilled fin sake.
